interactive.title: The venturi
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: This is a short lesson in thirteen small screens. The main picture is a level pipe full of seawater, seen from the side. It narrows to a throat in the middle. The pipe's bore is 20 cm². That is about the inside of a 50 mm pipe, since π × 2.5² is about 19.6 cm². Dots ride along with the water. A throat slider sets the throat's area. It runs from 4 to 20 cm² in steps of 1, and starts at 5. A flow slider sets the flow. It runs from 0 to 6 L/s in steps of 0.5, and starts at 4. Under each section a label shows area × speed. The flow is the same at every section. So the speed at a section is the flow ÷ its area. In the pipe, that is 0.004 m³/s ÷ 0.002 m², or 2.0 m/s. In the throat, it is 0.004 ÷ 0.0005, or 8.0 m/s. Both labels multiply out to 4.0 L/s. The dots are evenly spaced in the pipe. They stretch apart in the throat, because each one covers more ground each second there. One slug of water is picked out. An arrow on each end shows the pressure pushing on it. Going into the throat, the arrow behind it is longer than the one in front. That difference speeds it up. Leaving the throat, the arrows swap and it slows. Three thin columns stand on the pipe. One is before the throat, one is on it and one is after it. Each stands as high as the pressure under it can hold up, by ρgh. The pressure before the throat is held at 150 kPa gauge. So that column would stand about 14.9 m. It is drawn far shorter. The throat's pressure is lower by ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²). Seawater is taken at 1025 kg/m³. At the starting settings, that is ½ × 1025 × (8² − 2²), about 30.8 kPa. So the throat's column stands about 3.1 m lower. The column after the throat stands level with the first again, because the water slows back to 2.0 m/s. Three readouts wrap onto two rows on a phone. They show the throat's speed, the pressure drop from pipe to throat, and the flow worked back from that drop. To work it back, the drop gives the pipe's speed, v₁ = √(2 × drop ÷ (ρ × ((A₁ ÷ A₂)² − 1))). The flow is then A₁ × v₁. With the throat opened to the full 20 cm², there is no drop and nothing to measure. So that readout shows a dash. A small plot beside the pipe shows the drop against the flow. It rises as the flow squared. A dot marks the flow you have set. At the limits, 6 L/s through a 4 cm² throat, the speeds are 3.0 and 15.0 m/s. The drop is about 110.7 kPa. The throat's column still stands, at about 39.3 kPa. A measure switch hides the flow slider and the flow readout. Then you find the flow from the columns. A switch picks thick oil creeping or thin seawater moving fast. It swaps the dots for streamlines. The oil glides in smooth layers. The fast seawater churns in eddies. A Reynolds number scale below lights up to match. The words "the change comes somewhere between about 2000 and 4000, or higher" are written on it. Screen by screen. Screen 1 is a warm-up. Seawater runs at 2 m/s through a pipe of 20 cm². How many litres pass each second? 40 L/s, 4 L/s or 0.004 L/s. The 20 cm² is 0.002 m², so 0.002 × 2 = 0.004 m³ each second, which is 4 L/s. A right answer says "Still there." Screen 2 shows the dots streaming through. Both area × speed labels read 4.0 L/s. As the throat slider narrows the throat, the labels stay equal. Screen 3 asks for a prediction before the columns appear. The water speeds up from 2 to 8 m/s in the throat. How will the throat's column stand? The throat's column stands lowest. Or it stands tallest, because the water is squeezed there. Or all three stand level. Screen 4 shows the columns, with the picked-out slug and its two arrows. The throat's column stands lower, and the one after stands back up. Screen 5 asks a question. Water flows at 1.5 m/s in a pipe of 12 cm² and enters a section of 4 cm². How fast does it go there? 4.5 m/s, 0.5 m/s or 1.5 m/s. Screen 6 shows the energy at each section as a stacked bar of pressure plus ½ρv². Each adds to about 152 kPa. In the pipe it is 150 + 2.1. In the throat it is about 119.2 + 32.8. Screen 7 asks another. Seawater flows at 1 m/s in a pipe of 15 cm² into a throat of 5 cm². How much does the pressure change? About 4.1 kPa lower, about 4.6 kPa lower, or about 4.1 kPa higher. Screen 8 shows the flow slider and the plot. At 2 L/s the drop is about 7.7 kPa, a quarter of 30.8. At 6 L/s it is about 69.2 kPa. Screen 9 is the measure switch. The flow is hidden, and the throat is at 5 cm². The columns differ by about 7.7 kPa. What is the flow? 2 L/s, 1 L/s or 4 L/s. Screen 10 shows the switch, first thick oil in smooth layers, then fast seawater in eddies. Screen 11 asks which flow is most likely to run in smooth layers. Is it thick, cold oil creeping through a small pipe? Seawater at 2 m/s in a 50 mm pipe? Or the same seawater at the same speed in a 150 mm pipe? A right answer draws smooth layers in the oil only, the most likely of the three to run smooth. Screens 12 and 13 bring it all together. In screen 12, seawater flows at 3 L/s through a pipe of 15 cm², into a throat of 6 cm². How big is the drop? About 12.8 kPa, about 10.8 kPa or about 4.6 kPa. The speeds are 0.003 ÷ 0.0015 = 2 m/s and 0.003 ÷ 0.0006 = 5 m/s. So the drop is ½ × 1025 × (5² − 2²), about 10.8 kPa. Screen 13 gives a drop of 30.8 kPa in seawater. How much lower does the throat's column stand? About 3.1 m, about 0.3 m or about 30.8 m. Where it can be, a wrong pick is drawn on the picture. That way you see where it fails.
interactive.ignores: The pipe is level, so height plays no part. The water is taken as frictionless. So the column after the throat stands fully back up. A real venturi gets most of the drop back, not all of it. The rest is lost to friction. The speed is drawn the same across the pipe. Real water moves faster in the middle than at the walls. The seawater is taken as not squeezing at all. It has one density throughout. The columns are drawn far shorter than life. The pressure before the throat is held at 150 kPa whatever the flow. In a real system, the pump and the pipe set it. The smooth and eddying pictures are sketches, not a simulation. If a throat's pressure fell low enough, the water would boil there. Nothing in this picture's range comes near that.

explain.text:
Water speeds up where a pipe narrows. While it is there, its pressure drops. Both follow from two things you already trust. What goes in must come out. And energy is not made from nothing. Measure that drop, and the narrowing becomes a flow meter.

Start with what goes in. Water barely squeezes. So in a full pipe, every litre that enters pushes a litre out further along. The flow, in litres a second, is the same at every section.[^2] The flow through a section is its area × the water's average speed. Each second, a slug of water as long as that speed slides through that area. Take a pipe of 20 cm², which is 0.002 m², carrying water at 2 m/s. It passes 0.002 × 2 = 0.004 m³ each second. That is 4 L/s. Narrow it to a throat of 5 cm², a quarter of the area. The same 4 L/s must pass. So the water there moves four times as fast, at 8 m/s. That is [[continuity]]. Area × speed stays the same along the pipe. So A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.

Speeding up needs a push. Along a level pipe, the push comes from the pressure of the water around it. So going into the throat, each bit of water must have higher pressure behind it than in front. That means the pressure falls as the speed rises. As water flows into a narrower part, its speed and its kinetic energy go up.[^3] That energy comes out of the pressure. Pressure is itself energy per cubic metre. Pushing 1 m³ of water in against 1 Pa takes 1 J. Moving water also carries ½ρv² of kinetic energy in each cubic metre. Here ρ is its density and v its speed. Along a level pipe with no friction, the two add to the same total. So p + ½ρv² stays constant. That is [[Bernoulli's principle]]. A pipe that climbs adds a third share, the ρgh you met with pressure in liquids. So the throat's pressure is lower by ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²). Seawater is 1025 kg/m³.[^1] So here the drop is ½ × 1025 × (8² − 2²) = ½ × 1025 × 60, about 30.8 kPa. After the throat, the pipe widens. The water slows back to 2 m/s, and the pressure comes back. This is a teaching model with no friction. Real water has some. So a real venturi gets most of its drop back after the throat, not all of it. Many people expect the opposite, that faster water means higher pressure. A hose's jet hits hard because it is fast. Out in the air, the pressure inside the jet is only the air's.

Turn that round and you have a flow meter. The drop grows with the speed squared. The speed is in step with the flow. So twice the flow gives four times the drop. Measure the drop between the pipe and the throat, and you can work back to the speed, then the flow. A pipe narrowed smoothly and tapped for this is a [[venturi]].[^4] An orifice plate, a flat plate with a hole in it, measures flow the same way. A Pitot tube is another meter. It measures the water's speed.[^6] A sharp-edged orifice comes with a correction factor, its discharge coefficient.[^7] Through our pipe, 4 L/s gives a drop of about 30.8 kPa. Half the flow, 2 L/s, gives a quarter of that, about 7.7 kPa. The flow itself can glide in smooth layers or churn in eddies. Which you get depends on the speed, the bore and how thick the liquid is. Engineers roll these into one figure, the Reynolds number. Below about 2000, flow is smooth. Above about 4000, it usually eddies. Neither edge is fixed. Some put the upper one as high as 10 000. In between, a flow can go either way. Faster, wider and thinner flows are more likely to eddy.

**Through a narrowing, the same flow must go faster. The energy for that speed comes out of the pressure. So a venturi's pressure drop measures the flow.**

analogy.text: Think of one current through a cable with a thinner length spliced into it. The same amps pass every section of the cable, just as the same litres a second pass every section of the pipe. In the thin length, the current is crowded into less copper. So its current density, in amps per mm², goes up. The water's speed does the same in the throat. A voltmeter across the thin length reads a drop there. The columns show a drop at the throat in the same way.
analogy.breaks: A cable's drop across its thin length is lost as heat. The voltage never comes back further along. A venturi's drop is mostly not lost. It went into speed. It comes back as pressure when the pipe widens and the water slows. Only the friction part is lost, as in the cable. And a cable's volt drop is in step with the current, I × R. A venturi's drop goes with the flow squared.

practice.text:
**Safe first:** A flow meter's pressure tappings and their small pipes are part of the pressure system. Before you break into them, isolate and vent them, as for any pipe under pressure.

**Reading flow from a venturi**
- Find the pipe's area and the throat's area, in m². 1 cm² is 0.0001 m².
- Read the drop in pressure from pipe to throat, in Pa. A differential pressure gauge reads it directly.
- Work out the area ratio, pipe ÷ throat, and square it.
- Speed in the pipe: v₁ = √(2 × drop ÷ (ρ × (ratio² − 1))).
- Flow = the pipe's area × v₁, in m³/s. Multiply by 1000 for L/s.
- A real meter comes with its maker's correction factor. Multiply the flow by it.

**Rules of thumb:** The flow goes with the square root of the drop. Twice the flow gives four times the drop. So a meter reads poorly at low flow, because the drop there is tiny. In seawater, each 10 kPa of drop is about 1 m of column. An orifice plate is a flat plate with a hole in it. It works the same way.

**Worked example:** Seawater at 1025 kg/m³ runs through a pipe of 20 cm² with a throat of 5 cm². The gauge reads a drop of 7,700 Pa. The area ratio is 4. Squared, that is 16, and less 1 it is 15. So v₁ = √(2 × 7,700 ÷ (1025 × 15)), about 1.0 m/s. Flow = 0.002 × 1.0 = 0.002 m³/s. That is 2 L/s.

**Common mistakes**
- Expecting the pressure to rise where the pipe narrows. It falls, because the water is speeding up.
- Leaving out the pipe's own speed. The drop is ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²), not ½ρv₂².
- Subtracting the speeds before you square them.
- Treating the drop as in step with the flow. It goes with the flow squared.
- Mixing cm² and m².
- Expecting all of the drop to come back after the throat. A real meter loses a little to friction.

In an incompressible fluid, the flow rate at one point is the flow rate everywhere: area × speed in the throat equals the pipe's at every throat and flow
When a fluid flows into a narrower channel, its speed increases: each narrower throat gives a faster speed in it

Venturi flow meters work on the principles of the Bernoulli equation: pressure plus ½ρv² is the same in the pipe and the throat, and the flow worked back from the drop is the flow set, at every narrowed setting
Twice the flow gives four times the drop, at every throat

applied.problem: "Flow is area × the water's speed" holds only for one speed across the bore; real water runs faster in the middle than at the walls, so the rule is area × average speed, which is what Dan will need in i7's pipes.

The reading steps give the ideal, frictionless flow; a real venturi reads a little high by that formula and its maker's correction factor, just under 1, must be applied, so the job method is more certain than the explanation allows.
